carousel.body: Track the difference between the training score and the test score, not just the test score. A widening gap tells you the model has started to memorise.

sparks.hook: A plain algorithm with more data usually beats a clever one with less.
sparks.insight: Given a choice between a sophisticated learner trained on a little data and a simple learner trained on a lot, the simple one usually wins. Data supplies the constraints a model would otherwise have to guess at. This is why so much of the practical work in machine learning is really data work: collecting it, cleaning it, labelling it, deciding what a row means. The glamorous part is choosing an architecture, and it is rarely the part that decides the outcome.
sparks.why: The pattern has held for language and vision, and the decade after publication strengthened it through sheer scale. It has limits: bad labels do not average out, and duplicated data adds volume without information.
sparks.apply: Before tuning a model further, spend a day auditing a sample of your labels by hand. Count how many are wrong and fix the process that produced them.

sparks.hook: Add enough columns and everything becomes equally far from everything.
sparks.insight: Intuitions about nearness come from a world with three dimensions. In a space with hundreds of them, points spread towards the edges, distances between any two of them converge, and the notion of a nearest neighbour quietly stops meaning anything. Adding a feature that carries no signal actively harms methods that rely on similarity. This is why representation matters more than the algorithm on top: the useful work is finding a small number of dimensions where distance means something again.
sparks.why: The effect is geometric and unavoidable rather than an artefact of any one method. It is the main reason feature selection and learned embeddings buy more than a stronger classifier does.
sparks.apply: Count the features in your model against the number of examples per feature. If it is thin, cut features or learn a compressed representation before adding a bigger model.

sparks.hook: A model built on an assumption you know is false can still be the right choice.
sparks.insight: The naive Bayes classifier assumes every feature is independent of every other one given the class. In real text, real medicine and real anything, this is plainly untrue. The classifier works anyway, and for a specific reason: to pick the winning class you only need the ranking of the scores to come out right, not the probabilities themselves. So the errors caused by the false assumption often cancel out exactly where it matters. Useful is not the same as correct.
sparks.why: This is a well-documented result rather than a curiosity. The catch is that the probabilities it reports are badly calibrated, so a naive Bayes confidence score should never be read as a real likelihood.
sparks.apply: If you need a fast baseline for a text task, fit naive Bayes first and treat it as the bar. Judge every fancier model by how far it clears that bar.

sparks.hook: The hard part of learning is knowing which step deserves the blame.
sparks.insight: When a system with many stages produces a wrong answer, the difficulty is not noticing the error. It is deciding which of thousands of internal adjustments contributed to it, and by how much. Backpropagation solves this by pushing the error backwards through the network and computing each connection's share of the responsibility. That single trick is what makes deep networks trainable, and it is the reason one tribe moved from the margins to the centre of the field.
sparks.why: Credit assignment is the same problem in reinforcement learning, in organisations and in science. Backpropagation solves it only where the whole system is differentiable, which is a real restriction rather than a technicality.
sparks.apply: In your own work, find one outcome you measure but cannot attribute. Design a way to assign credit to the steps before you try to improve the outcome.

sparks.hook: Evolution is a search algorithm, and it needs no gradient at all.
sparks.insight: Genetic methods keep a population of candidate solutions, score them, keep the better ones, mix and mutate them, and repeat. The appeal is that they need nothing from the problem except a score, so they work where you cannot compute a direction of improvement: discrete structures, hardware layouts, programs, game strategies. The price is an enormous number of evaluations. This is the tribe that has commercially delivered the least, and it still owns corners where nothing else works.
sparks.why: Population search survives in hyperparameter tuning, architecture search and engineering design optimisation. The stronger claim, that it is a general path to intelligence, has not been borne out.
sparks.apply: When your objective is not differentiable, stop hunting for a gradient method. Score candidates, keep the top slice, perturb them, and repeat for a fixed budget.

sparks.hook: The bet was on unification. What arrived was scale.
sparks.insight: The central proposal is that the five traditions could be fused into one algorithm capable of learning anything from data. Since 2015 the field went a different way. One tradition, neural networks, absorbed enormous amounts of data and computation and took over tasks the other tribes had owned. There is partial vindication in that a single architecture now covers vision, language and audio. There is no unified learner in the sense proposed, and the winning approach did not come from blending the five.
sparks.why: This is a scoreboard rather than a criticism from outside. The framing remains the clearest introduction to the field even where its central forecast has been overtaken by what actually happened next.
sparks.apply: Read it for the map of ideas, then read a recent survey of transformer-based models to see which parts of that map are now largely empty.

sparks.hook: Every recommendation you receive is a guess about a model of you.
sparks.insight: Firms hold a rough statistical model of your behaviour and use it to decide what you see, what you pay and sometimes whether you are approved. The argument here is that this model should belong to you, so you could point it at your own goals instead of theirs. That has not happened. Data portability rules let you export records in some countries, but a bundle of exported rows is not the same thing as owning the model that was learned from them.
sparks.why: The gap between exporting data and controlling a model is the whole difficulty, and it has not narrowed since publication. Treat the proposal as a useful frame rather than as a live option.
sparks.apply: Export your data from one large platform and read what is actually there. Note what it reveals about you that you never typed in directly.

actions: Take one model in production near you and name its tribe, its core assumption, and the kind of data that would break it.
Set up an honest evaluation before your next experiment: a held-out test set you touch once, and a tracked gap between training and test scores.
Spend a day on data quality rather than model choice. Sample your labels, count the errors, and fix the process that produced them.
Read a current survey of large neural models alongside this one, so you can see which of the five tribes actually won the decade.
not_for_you_if: You want code, maths or a practical tutorial. This is a conceptual tour with no implementation detail, and its central prediction about a unifying algorithm has not aged well.

verification.notes: First published September 2015 by Basic Books. Sparks flag that the proposed unification did not arrive and that scaled neural networks took the field in a different direction. All prose is original.

title: Code
subtitle: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
author: Charles Petzold
why_it_matters: It builds a working computer in front of you from switches and wire, with no step you have to take on trust. Almost nothing else closes the gap between electricity and software, and it does so without requiring any real mathematics.

crux.headline: A computer is switches wired to flip each other
crux.body: Start with the fact that any two distinguishable states can encode anything, given enough of them. Add a switch that electricity can operate rather than a finger. Wire those switches into logic, logic into arithmetic, arithmetic into a machine that reads its own instructions out of memory. Every layer is simple and the tower of them is a computer. Once you have climbed it, no part of a machine can intimidate you again.

sparks.hook: Two children with torches across a street invent binary by accident.
sparks.insight: If the only thing you can do is switch a light on and off, you can still send any message, provided you and the receiver agree on a code and are willing to spend enough flashes. Morse did it with short and long. Braille did it with raised and flat. The number of symbols you need grows as you add more possible meanings, and that trade between alphabet size and message length is the whole idea behind binary. Computers took the least expressive alphabet available and made up the difference with speed.
sparks.why: Codes predate electronics by a century, which is the point. Binary is not a computer thing, it is the minimum viable alphabet, and everything above it is a convention layered on top.
sparks.apply: Write your initials in binary using five bits per letter. It takes two minutes and permanently removes the mystery from the phrase machine code.

sparks.hook: One bit is exactly one answer to one yes-or-no question.
sparks.insight: A bit is not so much a tiny amount of data as a decision. Each one you receive cuts the space of possibilities in half. Two bits pick one of four things, eight bits pick one of two hundred and fifty-six, and ten bits already separate more than a thousand. This is why file sizes and address widths behave the way they do, and why adding a bit doubles what you can name rather than adding one more option to the list.
sparks.why: Counting possibilities rather than storing values is the information-theoretic view of a bit. It makes memory sizes, address spaces and encodings predictable instead of arbitrary.
sparks.apply: Next time you meet a limit like 255 or 65535, work out the bit width behind it. Most odd-looking software limits are a power of two minus one.

sparks.hook: The whole trick is a switch that another switch can flip.
sparks.insight: A hand-operated switch does nothing a person could not do themselves. A relay is different: current through one circuit pulls a lever that closes another circuit. Now the output of one switching decision can be the input of the next, and you can chain them without a human in the loop. Telegraph engineers built relays to repeat signals down long lines, not to compute anything. Once that component exists, arithmetic and memory become a question of wiring.
sparks.why: This is the actual hinge between electricity and computation. Vacuum tubes and transistors are faster versions of the same idea, a switch controlled by a signal rather than by a finger.
sparks.apply: Sketch two relays in series and two in parallel, and label what each pair outputs. You have just drawn an AND gate and an OR gate from scratch.

sparks.hook: Series means and. Parallel means or. That is most of logic.
sparks.insight: Nineteenth-century logic was written as an algebra of true and false long before anyone could build it out of anything. Wire two switches one after the other and current flows only if both are closed, which is conjunction. Wire them side by side and it flows if either is closed, which is disjunction. Add an arrangement that outputs the opposite of its input and you have negation. Those three operations express any logical function at all, which means they can build any circuit at all.
sparks.why: Boolean algebra came from George Boole in the 1850s and was connected to switching circuits by Claude Shannon in the 1930s. The completeness of and, or and not is a proved property, not a convention.
sparks.apply: Take a rule from your own work stated in words with ands and ors, and redraw it as a gate diagram. Ambiguities in the wording become visible immediately.

carousel.title: Series is AND
carousel.body: Two switches one after another. Current arrives only when both are closed. This is the circuit form of requiring every condition to hold at the same time.

carousel.title: Parallel is OR
carousel.body: Two switches side by side, either path sufficient. Current arrives when at least one is closed. This is the circuit form of accepting any of several conditions.

carousel.title: Invert for NOT
carousel.body: Arrange a relay so that energising it breaks the circuit rather than completing it. The output becomes the opposite of the input, and that reversal completes the set.

carousel.title: Combine for anything
carousel.body: Any truth table you can write down can be built from those three operations. There is no fourth idea waiting later, only larger arrangements of these three.

sparks.hook: You can add two numbers with nothing but switches and patience.
sparks.insight: Adding one bit to another gives a result bit and possibly a carry, which is two logic functions of two inputs. Build that once and you have the smallest adder there is. Chain eight of them so each carry feeds the next column, exactly as you were taught to do addition on paper, and the machine adds eight-bit numbers. Nothing is hidden here: no arithmetic unit arrives by magic, only gates arranged to reproduce a procedure children already know.
sparks.why: Every arithmetic operation in a processor descends from this construction. Subtraction is addition with a complemented operand, and multiplication is repeated shifted addition.
sparks.apply: Draw the truth table for one bit plus one bit with a carry in and a carry out. Build it from and, or and not before reading how anyone else did it.

sparks.hook: Wire a gate's output back into its own input and it starts remembering.
sparks.insight: Feedback turns a circuit that only reacts into a circuit that holds. Connect two gates so that each drives the other and the pair settles into one of two stable states, staying there until something pushes it. That is one bit of memory, made from the same components as the logic. Stack them into rows, add circuitry to select a row by number, and you have exactly what random access memory is. Storage is not a different kind of thing from computation.
sparks.why: Bistability from feedback is the mechanism behind static memory. Dynamic memory instead holds charge in tiny capacitors, which is why it has to be refreshed constantly to avoid forgetting.
sparks.apply: Explain to someone how a light switch differs from a doorbell. The switch stays where you put it, and that difference is the difference between memory and logic.

sparks.hook: Hexadecimal is not a harder number system. It is binary for humans.
sparks.insight: Counting in tens is an accident of having ten fingers, not a property of numbers. Any base works the same way: each position is worth the base times the position to its right. Long runs of binary are unreadable, so engineers group four bits at a time and give each group a single symbol, which yields sixteen symbols and hexadecimal. A hex digit is not a translation of binary, it is the same bits written more compactly for a human eye.
sparks.why: The grouping works cleanly because sixteen is a power of two. That is why memory addresses, colour codes and byte dumps are shown in hex rather than in decimal.
sparks.apply: Convert one colour code from your stylesheet into its three byte values and then into binary. The notation stops feeling arbitrary once you have done it once.

sparks.hook: Instructions live in the same memory as data and look identical.
sparks.insight: A processor reads a number from memory, treats it as a command, does what it says, and moves to the next address. The number meaning add and the number meaning the quantity forty-two are indistinguishable in storage; only the context in which they are fetched decides which is which. That single design choice is what makes a computer general rather than a fixed machine, because a program can be loaded, changed, or written by another program.
sparks.why: This is the stored-program idea behind the machine designs of the 1940s. It also explains a whole family of security failures, in which data supplied by an attacker ends up executed as instructions.
sparks.apply: Read any explanation of a buffer overflow with this in mind. The attack works because the machine cannot tell your instructions from your input without help.

sparks.hook: Every layer of a computer exists to let you forget the one below it.
sparks.insight: Nobody thinks about relays while writing a web page, and that is an achievement rather than a gap in their education. Each layer takes the mess underneath and offers a smaller, cleaner set of things you can say. The cost is that when a layer leaks, and they all leak eventually, you need at least one floor of knowledge below where you normally live. Learning the ladder once means every future confusion has a floor you can descend to.
sparks.why: Abstraction is the only reason a system this complex can be built by people at all. It is also why bugs that cross layers are the hardest ones to diagnose and the slowest to fix.
sparks.apply: Pick a bug that baffled you recently and work out which layer it actually lived in. Then spend a weekend learning one layer below that one.

carousel.title: Switches
carousel.body: A component that opens or closes a circuit under the control of another circuit. Relay, valve or transistor, the role is identical and only the speed changes.

carousel.title: Gates
carousel.body: Small groups of switches that compute and, or and not. At this layer you stop thinking about electricity and start thinking about true and false.

carousel.title: Arithmetic and memory
carousel.body: Gates arranged into adders that calculate and into feedback loops that hold state. The machine can now both compute a value and remember what it computed.

carousel.title: Instructions
carousel.body: A fetch and execute loop that pulls numbers from memory and treats them as commands. The machine becomes general purpose rather than purpose-built.

carousel.title: Languages
carousel.body: Text that a program translates into those instructions, so people can express intent instead of opcodes. Every layer above this one is more of the same move.

sparks.hook: Bits mean nothing by themselves. Meaning is an agreement.
sparks.insight: The same eight bits are a small number, a letter, a shade of grey or a fragment of sound depending only on what the reading program has agreed to assume. Text encodings, image formats and audio samples are conventions that were written down and adopted, not properties of the data. This is why a file opened with the wrong program produces garbage rather than an error, and why encoding bugs are so persistent: nothing in the bits announces what they were meant to be.
sparks.why: Character encoding history is a long series of incompatible agreements, which is why text handling remains a common source of production bugs decades after the problem was understood.
sparks.apply: Open a small image or text file in a hex viewer. Find the header bytes that tell software which convention to apply, then look up what they mean.

actions: Draw the ladder from switch to programming language on one page, with a single sentence per layer, and keep it where you work.
Build a one-bit adder on paper from and, or and not gates, then extend it to four bits with carries running between the columns.
Open a file in a hex viewer, identify its header, and work out how the format tells a program what the rest of the bytes mean.
Pick the layer of the stack you understand least and spend a weekend one floor below where you normally work.
not_for_you_if: You want current material on operating systems, networks or machine learning. The climb ends at older hardware, and the pace drags if you already know digital logic.

verification.notes: First published 1999 by Microsoft Press; a substantially revised second edition appeared in 2022 with rewritten later chapters. The year given is first publication. All prose is original.

title: The Pragmatic Programmer
subtitle: From Journeyman to Master
author: Andrew Hunt and David Thomas
why_it_matters: It gave a generation of programmers a shared vocabulary for craft that is still spoken in code review twenty-five years later. The specific tooling advice has dated badly; the habits of mind underneath it have not.

crux.headline: Every decision is a bet on what will change
crux.body: The trade is not typing, it is judgement under uncertainty. You never know which requirement will move, so you make choices that keep options open: one authoritative home for each piece of knowledge, components that can be changed without disturbing their neighbours, decisions that are cheap to reverse. Add the habit of fixing small rot before it spreads, and the discipline of knowing why your code works rather than accepting that it does.

sparks.hook: One tolerated mess gives everyone permission for the next one.
sparks.insight: A codebase with a few known bad patches does not stay at a few. Once a file is visibly neglected, the next person under pressure adds their own shortcut, because the cost of being the one who lowered the standard has already been paid by somebody else. The decay is social rather than technical. The countermeasure is small and immediate: fix the broken thing now, or at minimum board it up visibly with a ticket and a note, so it reads as damage rather than as the house style.
sparks.why: The analogy is borrowed from broken windows criminology, which is contested and whose policing applications are heavily disputed. For code the claim rests on the ordinary observation that standards get copied from whatever is already there.
sparks.apply: In the next file you open, fix one small thing that is obviously wrong before you start your actual task. Keep it to five minutes.

sparks.hook: Every piece of knowledge should have exactly one home in your system.
sparks.insight: Duplication is dangerous not because typing twice is wasteful but because the two copies will drift. Someone updates one and misses the other, and now the system holds two contradictory beliefs about the same fact. The rule applies to knowledge rather than to characters: a validation rule expressed in the database, the API and the form is three copies of one decision. Two functions that merely look similar but encode unrelated decisions are not duplication at all.
sparks.why: The rule is widely over-applied. Deduplicating code that only looks alike couples things that change for different reasons, and many experienced engineers now hold that a little duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
sparks.apply: Find a rule in your system expressed in more than one place. Move it to a single source and generate or derive the other copies from that one.

sparks.hook: Ask how many files you must touch to change one thing.
sparks.insight: Two components are orthogonal when changing one does not require changing the other. It is the property that decides whether a system stays workable as it grows, and it is measurable: pick a plausible change and count what it touches. If swapping a database forces edits in your user interface, those two are entangled. Orthogonal designs also fail more usefully, because a broken part damages a bounded region instead of everything downstream from it.
sparks.why: Coupling grows quietly, since every shortcut that reaches across a boundary saves time today and charges on every future change. Counting touched files turns an invisible property into a number.
sparks.apply: Name three changes your product is likely to need next year. For each, count the files you would have to edit. The largest count is your next refactor.

sparks.hook: Build the thinnest thing that runs end to end, then thicken it.
sparks.insight: Rather than finishing one layer at a time and integrating at the end, connect every layer at once with the smallest possible path through them: one request, one record, one screen, no features. You learn immediately whether the architecture holds, and everyone can see something working. This differs from a prototype, which exists to answer a question and is then thrown away. A thin path is production code from the start, just extremely narrow.
sparks.why: Integration risk is the risk that appears in no component's tests. Finding it in week one rather than month six is the whole benefit, and it is why the practice survived into continuous delivery.
sparks.apply: For your next project, ship a single end-to-end path to a real environment in the first week, even if it does almost nothing useful yet.

carousel.title: Pick one narrow path
carousel.body: Choose the single most representative journey through the system. One input, one transformation, one output. Resist adding a second case until the first one runs.

carousel.title: Wire every layer
carousel.body: Touch every real component the finished system will use, including deployment. A path that skips the queue or the database has not tested the risky part.

carousel.title: Keep it production shaped
carousel.body: Write it as code you intend to keep, with tests and error handling. If it is throwaway quality you have built a prototype and learned much less.

carousel.title: Thicken along the line
carousel.body: Add features by widening the path that already works, so the system is always integrated. Each addition ships instead of waiting for one big merge.

sparks.hook: Explain the bug out loud to something that cannot possibly help.
sparks.insight: Describing a problem in full sentences to a colleague, a pet or an inanimate object solves a surprising share of them before the listener has said anything. Reading code lets your brain skip; narrating it forces every step into sequence and exposes the one you have been assuming rather than checking. The listener's ignorance is the useful part, because it obliges you to state the context you have been carrying silently in your head.
sparks.why: The mechanism is that explanation forces serial, explicit processing, the same reason writing clarifies thinking. It is a technique rather than a research finding, but it costs nothing to test.
sparks.apply: Next time you are stuck for more than twenty minutes, say the problem out loud from the beginning, including everything you have already ruled out.

sparks.hook: It works is not the same as I know why it works.
sparks.insight: Code that was assembled by trial and error and kept because a run finally succeeded is a trap. You do not know which of your changes mattered, so you cannot predict what will break it. The behaviour you relied on may be an accident of the current implementation rather than a promise of the interface. Deliberate programming means being able to say why each line is there, and being suspicious when something starts working for no reason you can state.
sparks.why: Undocumented behaviour changes without warning, and a fix nobody can explain gets undone by the next person tidying up. The cost lands later, which is why the habit is hard to keep under deadline.
sparks.apply: When something starts working unexpectedly, do not move on. Break it again deliberately to confirm you know which change was responsible.

sparks.hook: Most debugging time is spent confidently fixing the wrong thing.
sparks.insight: Panic and guessing are the expensive parts of debugging, and a routine removes both. Reproduce the failure reliably before touching anything, because a fix you cannot verify is a coincidence. Read the actual error rather than the one you expected. Narrow the space by halves instead of hunting, and check your assumptions about the data before you start doubting the compiler. Most bugs are in your own recent changes, and the routine gets you there faster than intuition.
sparks.why: Bisecting through the change history or the code path is the fastest general strategy, because each test removes half of the remaining candidates regardless of where the fault turns out to be.
sparks.apply: Write your team's debugging checklist on one card: reproduce, read, isolate by halves, verify the fix, add the test that would have caught it.

carousel.title: Reproduce it first
carousel.body: Find the smallest reliable way to trigger the failure. Without a repeatable case you cannot tell a fix from a coincidence, and you will not know when you are done.

carousel.title: Read what it actually says
carousel.body: Read the whole error and the whole stack trace, not the first line. A large share of debugging time goes on problems the message had already named.

carousel.title: Halve the space
carousel.body: Bisect: revert to a known good commit, disable half the code, or cut the input in two. Ten halvings cover more than a thousand candidates.

carousel.title: Doubt yourself first
carousel.body: Suspect your own recent change before the framework, the compiler or the operating system. Verify assumptions about the data with a print rather than a belief.

carousel.title: Leave a test behind
carousel.body: Once it is fixed, write the test that would have caught it. Otherwise the same class of bug returns and you pay for the entire investigation twice.

sparks.hook: Answering in days implies a precision that answering in months does not.
sparks.insight: The unit you choose is itself a claim about your confidence. Say six months and people hear a date; say two quarters and they hear a range. Beyond the units, the honest method is to break work into pieces small enough that you have done something similar before, estimate those, and record what actually happened so the next estimate has evidence behind it. An estimate given without a record of your past errors is a guess wearing a suit.
sparks.why: Estimates are systematically optimistic because we imagine the path where nothing goes wrong. Tracking your historical ratio of estimate to actual corrects for that far better than trying harder to be accurate.
sparks.apply: Log your next five estimates and their actual durations. Multiply future estimates by the ratio you observe rather than by a number you like.

sparks.hook: A program that stops at the first impossible state loses the least.
sparks.insight: When something happens that you believed could not happen, continuing is the expensive choice. The program is now operating on assumptions you know to be false, and every further step writes more damage into more places. Stopping immediately gives you the failure close to its cause, where the stack trace still points at something useful. Defensive code that quietly swallows the impossible converts one clear bug into an intermittent mystery discovered three systems away.
sparks.why: The cost of an error grows with the distance between where it happens and where it is noticed. Assertions and early failure compress that distance to nearly nothing.
sparks.apply: Add an assertion for one condition you consider impossible in a critical path. If it never fires you lost nothing; if it fires you found something real.

sparks.hook: Your skills are a portfolio and some of them are depreciating.
sparks.insight: Skills lose value on a schedule you do not control. A framework that guaranteed employment can become a maintenance niche within a few years, so treating learning as an occasional burst leaves you concentrated in assets that are quietly falling. The suggestion is to invest regularly and in small amounts, diversify across areas that fail at different times, and take a deliberate position in something unproven, sized so that being wrong costs you a few weekends.
sparks.why: The portfolio framing is an analogy rather than evidence, and prescriptions such as learning a new language every year are folklore. The underlying point about regular small investment is sound.
sparks.apply: Book two hours a week in your calendar for learning outside your current stack, and choose something likely to still exist in ten years.

actions: Pick the three changes your system is most likely to need next year and count how many files each one would touch.

Write your team's debugging checklist on one card and use it the next three times you are stuck for more than twenty minutes.

not_for_you_if: You want depth in one language or modern cloud practice. Several tooling chapters have dated, and the twentieth anniversary edition rewrites much of that material.
